meta.subject: SEMINAR
meta.author: bank-team-seminar
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Narrow a broad research topic into a focused question
questions.stem: A translator notes the phrase covers too much ground; which move best narrows it without losing the core aim?

options.text: Add a population, period, and outcome to bound the inquiry precisely.
Replace the whole topic with a single case study of one author only.
options.misconception: narrows to one example and drops the question

options.text: Keep every subtopic listed so nothing is lost from the original scope.
options.misconception: treats breadth as a virtue to preserve

options.text: Delete the topic and start from a fresh unrelated research question.

questions.explanation: Bounded scope keeps the core aim while making the question answerable; keeping breadth or jumping to one case both fail the narrowing test.

questions.learningObjective: Check whether a question can be answered with on-hand evidence
questions.stem: Maria's memo asks whether the 1890 census can settle a claim about migration; explain what makes it answerable or not.

answer.exemplar: A question is answerable only when the evidence contains the needed variables for the stated period; the 1890 census lacks occupation detail, so the claim about occupational migration cannot be settled without another source.

questions.explanation: Answerability depends on whether the source records the variables and period in question; missing occupation data blocks this particular claim.

questions.learningObjective: Spot a question that smuggles its answer

stimulus.body: The translator's note reads: why did the reform fail to help workers? The note assumes the reform failed and that workers were its target.

questions.stem: Which revision removes the presupposition while keeping the inquiry open?

options.text: Why did the reform fail to help workers at all?
Did the reform change workers' outcomes, and in what direction?
How badly did the reform harm workers overall?
Was the reform ever intended for workers?
options.misconception: shifts to intent and drops outcomes

questions.explanation: An open question asks what happened and in which direction; wording that assumes failure or harm closes off answers the evidence might support.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a term that must be defined before argument
questions.stem: Before debating whether a policy is fair, which term in the memo most needs an explicit definition first?

options.text: The date the policy was enacted, since dates anchor the debate.
The number of pages in the bill, since length signals complexity.
The name of the sponsoring committee, since names carry weight.
The word fair, since parties may use different standards of justice.

questions.explanation: Normative terms like fair carry competing standards; fixing a definition prevents talking past each other, while dates and names need no such fix.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a term that does not translate across fields
questions.stem: The memo borrows a term from economics into literary criticism; what risk does that carry?

options.text: The term may carry technical baggage that distorts the literary claim.
The term will always be rejected by journal editors on sight.
The term makes the argument shorter and therefore clearer.
The term guarantees the argument is interdisciplinary and strong.

questions.explanation: Borrowed vocabulary can import assumptions from its home field; the risk is distortion, not automatic rejection or guaranteed strength.

questions.topic: Assumptions carried by a borrowed method
questions.learningObjective: Name an assumption a borrowed method brings along
questions.stem: A memo adopts a survey method from sociology; which assumption must be checked before use?

options.text: That the memo's author prefers short paragraphs.
That the survey was printed on recycled paper.
That respondents answer honestly under all conditions.
That the journal requires double spacing.

questions.explanation: Borrowed methods carry assumptions about respondents and context; checking honesty conditions matters, while paper or formatting do not.

questions.learningObjective: Mark the limit of an analogy
questions.stem: The memo compares a city to a living organism; where does that analogy stop carrying weight?

answer.exemplar: The analogy helps with growth and interdependence but stops at intention and planning, since a city has deliberate design while an organism does not, so claims about purpose need other support.

questions.explanation: Analogies illuminate some features and mislead on others; purpose and planning are not organism traits, so those claims need independent grounds.

questions.topic: The warrant joining claim to reason
questions.learningObjective: Identify the warrant linking reason to claim
questions.stem: In the memo, the reason is rising rents and the claim is that families leave; what is the warrant?

options.text: Leaving is the only possible response.
Families prefer suburbs regardless of cost.
Rents always rise every single year.
Rising rents make staying unaffordable for most families.

questions.explanation: The warrant is the bridge showing why the reason supports the claim; affordability links rent to departure without adding unsupported generalizations.

questions.topic: Unstated premises a reader must supply
questions.learningObjective: Surface a hidden premise a reader supplies

stimulus.body: The translator's note argues that since the bridge is closed, commuters will be late, assuming commuters use that bridge.

questions.stem: Which unstated premise must the reader supply for the note to work?

options.text: Commuters always leave early enough to absorb delays.
The closed bridge is the usual route for those commuters.
All bridges in the city are closed at once.
Commuters never check traffic reports before leaving.

questions.explanation: The argument needs the bridge to be the usual route; without that, the closure does not imply lateness.

questions.learningObjective: Reject a conclusion that the premises do not support
questions.stem: Given that a book sold well, which conclusion in the memo does not follow?

options.text: The book reached many readers quickly.
The publisher earned revenue from it.
The book's ideas are therefore true.
Demand exceeded initial print run.

questions.explanation: Sales show reach and revenue, not truth; popularity does not validate an idea's content.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize an objection that adds new content
questions.stem: A critic objects to the memo's plan by introducing a cost no one mentioned; what kind of objection is this?

options.text: An objection that merely repeats the conclusion in new words.
An objection that changes the subject entirely.
An objection that denies the premise without reason.
An objection that adds a new consideration to the debate.

questions.explanation: Introducing an unmentioned cost adds to the debate rather than repeating or merely denying; it is additive.

questions.learningObjective: Decide between two incompatible readings
questions.stem: Two translators read the same line differently; what best adjudicates between them?

options.text: Choose the reading that flatters the translator's own view.
Always pick the shorter reading by default.
Prefer the reading supported by the surrounding textual evidence.
Defer to whichever translator is more senior.

questions.explanation: Adjudication rests on evidence in context, not on bias, length, or seniority.

questions.topic: Weight carried by primary and secondary sources
questions.learningObjective: Weigh primary against secondary sources
questions.stem: The memo cites both a diary and a later historian; which carries more weight for the author's intent?

answer.exemplar: The diary as a primary source carries more weight for authorial intent because it is contemporary, while the historian's account is useful for context but filtered through later interpretation.

questions.explanation: Primary sources are closer to the event and intent; secondary sources add context but carry interpretive distance.

questions.learningObjective: Write a summary that keeps argument structure
questions.stem: Which summary best preserves the memo's argument structure?

options.text: A summary that lists only the conclusion and omits reasons.
A summary that reorders points alphabetically.
A summary that adds the reader's own opinion.
A summary that keeps conclusion, reasons, and their order.

questions.explanation: Preserving structure means keeping the conclusion, reasons, and their sequence; omitting or reordering breaks the argument.

questions.topic: Holding a position at its strongest
questions.learningObjective: State an opposing view at its strongest

stimulus.body: The translator's note sets out the rival view in its fullest and most charitable form before replying.

questions.stem: Why state the rival view at its strongest before answering it?

options.text: To ensure the reply addresses the best version, not a straw man.
To make the reply look more impressive by contrast.
To avoid citing any sources in the reply.
To shorten the overall memo length.

questions.explanation: Charitable restatement prevents straw-manning; the reply then targets the strongest version rather than a weakened caricature.

questions.learningObjective: Rebuild the strongest version of a rejected view
questions.stem: When reconstructing the view the memo rejects, what should the translator include?

options.text: Only the weakest points so the rejection seems easy.
Personal attacks on the view's supporters.
The view's best premises and its intended conclusion.
Unrelated facts that make it look worse.

questions.explanation: A fair reconstruction includes the view's best premises and conclusion; weakening or attacking supporters misrepresents it.

questions.topic: Sympathetic reading of a weak argument
questions.learningObjective: Read a weak argument charitably
questions.stem: A memo's argument is flawed; what does a sympathetic reading require?

options.text: Ignore the flaws and accept the conclusion.
Dismiss the author as careless.
Rewrite the argument to match your own view.
Find the plausible aim behind the flawed reasoning.

questions.explanation: Sympathetic reading seeks the plausible aim or insight behind flawed reasoning without abandoning critique.

questions.topic: Citations that let a reader find the claim
questions.learningObjective: Write citations that locate a claim
questions.stem: Which citation in the memo lets a reader actually find the claim?

options.text: A full citation with author, title, and page range.
A vague reference to a well-known author with no page.
A mention that the idea is common knowledge.
A footnote that only says see above.

questions.explanation: A usable citation gives author, title, and page so the reader can locate the claim; vague or circular references fail.

questions.topic: Narrowing a topic in two steps
questions.learningObjective: Apply a two-step narrowing to a topic
questions.stem: Describe the two steps the memo uses to narrow a broad topic into a researchable question.

answer.exemplar: First delimit the population and period to shrink the scope, then specify the outcome or variable to be measured, producing a focused question that can be answered with available evidence.

questions.explanation: Two-step narrowing first bounds scope by population and period, then fixes the outcome variable, yielding an answerable question.

questions.learningObjective: Order the steps of framing a question
questions.stem: Which sequence best frames a research question according to the memo?

options.text: Answer first, then choose the topic, then define terms.
Cite sources first, then invent a question.
Narrow topic, define terms, check answerability, then refine.
Conclude first, then find supporting reasons.

questions.explanation: Framing proceeds from narrowing to definition to answerability check to refinement; answering or concluding first reverses inquiry.

questions.learningObjective: Detect a term shifting sense mid-argument

stimulus.body: The translator's note uses free first to mean no cost, then later to mean unconstrained, without flagging the change.

questions.stem: What fallacy or flaw does the note commit?

options.text: It keeps the term's sense stable throughout.
It removes the term entirely from the second use.
It defines the term twice in the same sentence.
It shifts the term's sense without warning, risking equivocation.

questions.explanation: Using a term in two senses without flagging it risks equivocation; the flaw is the unmarked shift, not definition or removal.

questions.topic: Two options presented as the whole field
questions.learningObjective: Spot a false dilemma
questions.stem: The memo presents only two policy options; what is the risk?

options.text: A third viable option may be excluded from consideration.
The two options might both be acceptable compromises.
Presenting two options always speeds up decisions.
Two options guarantee a balanced debate.

questions.explanation: Presenting two options as the whole field risks excluding viable alternatives; speed or balance do not justify the omission.

questions.learningObjective: Detect circular reasoning
questions.stem: The memo concludes that a source is reliable because it is trustworthy; what flaw is this?

options.text: A conclusion supported by independent evidence.
An appeal to a larger sample size.
Circular reasoning that uses the conclusion as a premise.
A rebuttal of an opposing view.

questions.explanation: Using trustworthy to prove reliable and reliable to prove trustworthy is circular; it lacks independent support.

questions.topic: Generalising from too small a base
questions.learningObjective: Reject an overgeneralization from small sample
questions.stem: The memo generalizes from three interviews; what is the problem?

options.text: Three interviews always suffice for any topic.
The memo should have used a survey instead.
Interviews are never useful evidence.
The base is too small to support a broad generalization.

questions.explanation: A handful of interviews cannot support a broad claim; the issue is sample size, not the method itself or a mandatory switch.

questions.topic: When an appeal to authority holds
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate when authority is a valid reason
questions.stem: Explain when an appeal to authority in the memo is legitimate rather than fallacious.

answer.exemplar: An appeal to authority holds when the authority is genuinely expert in the relevant field and the claim falls within that expertise, and when the authority's view is not the only evidence offered.

questions.explanation: Authority counts when expertise matches the claim and is not the sole support; expertise outside the field or lone reliance weakens it.

questions.topic: What the crowd does as a reason
questions.learningObjective: Assess an appeal to popularity

stimulus.body: The translator's note argues that many people believe the claim, so it must be true.

questions.stem: What is wrong with the note's reasoning?

options.text: Popularity does not establish truth of the claim.
Popular belief can be evidence of cultural trends.
The note cites too many sources.
Belief surveys are always invalid.

questions.explanation: Many people believing something shows prevalence, not truth; the flaw is treating popularity as proof.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish sequence from causation
questions.stem: The memo notes a policy change followed by growth; what must be established before claiming cause?

options.text: That growth occurred after the change.
That the policy change was popular.
That no other factor explains the growth.
That growth is always desirable.

questions.explanation: Temporal order alone does not imply causation; other explanations must be ruled out before claiming the change caused growth.

questions.topic: Revising a claim so it can be answered
questions.learningObjective: Revise an unanswerable claim into a testable one
questions.stem: How should the memo revise 'the policy is unfair' to make it answerable?

options.text: Keep it as is because fairness is self-evident.
Ask readers to vote on whether it is unfair.
Replace unfair with bad to simplify wording.
Specify the criterion, group, and comparison used to judge fairness.

questions.explanation: A testable revision defines the criterion, affected group, and comparison; vague swaps or votes do not make it answerable.

questions.learningObjective: Detect cherry-picking in a memo
questions.stem: The memo cites only studies supporting its view; what flaw is this?

options.text: Selective use of evidence that ignores contrary findings.
A thorough literature review.
Too many citations overall.
Use of secondary rather than primary sources.

questions.explanation: Citing only supporting studies while ignoring contrary findings is selective evidence; the flaw is omission, not quantity or source type.

questions.topic: A term carrying two senses across a passage
questions.learningObjective: Resolve a term with two senses
questions.stem: The word bank appears as riverbank and financial bank; how should the translator handle it?

answer.exemplar: The translator should mark the two senses explicitly and avoid letting one sense's connotations bleed into the other, perhaps by glossing or choosing a clearer term.

questions.explanation: A term with two senses needs explicit marking so connotations from one sense do not distort the other.

questions.learningObjective: Assign the burden of proof
questions.stem: In the memo's dispute, who bears the burden of proof?

options.text: Whoever makes the stronger-sounding claim.
The party with fewer citations.
The party introducing a new or unusual claim.
The reader, who must disprove it.

questions.explanation: The burden falls on whoever advances a new or unusual claim; strength, citation count, and reader disproof are not the standard.

questions.topic: Naming a fault and repairing it
questions.learningObjective: Name and repair an argument fault

stimulus.body: The translator's note spots a non sequitur and proposes replacing the unsupported conclusion with one the premises actually support.

questions.stem: What does the note do correctly?

options.text: It deletes all premises to avoid the fault.
It ignores the fault and keeps the conclusion.
It attacks the author instead of the argument.
It names the fault and offers a supported replacement.

questions.explanation: Naming the fault and replacing the conclusion with one the premises support is the correct repair; ignoring, attacking, or deleting all premises is not.

questions.learningObjective: Identify begging the question
questions.stem: The memo assumes what it sets out to prove; what is this called?

options.text: A strong inductive generalization.
A valid deductive proof.
Begging the question.
An appeal to common sense.

questions.explanation: Assuming the conclusion as a premise is begging the question; it is neither strong induction nor valid deduction.

questions.topic: Statements that can be argued about
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish arguable from non-arguable statements
questions.stem: Which statement in the memo can genuinely be argued about?

options.text: The report was published on March 3.
The document has twelve pages.
The author's name is printed on the cover.
The policy is unjustified given its costs and benefits.

questions.explanation: A statement combining costs and benefits is arguable; publication dates, names, and page counts are verifiable facts.

questions.topic: Sequence for building a sourced argument
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps of a sourced argument
questions.stem: Which sequence best builds a sourced argument?

options.text: Pose question, gather evidence, weigh it, then argue.
Conclude, then find evidence, then arrange reasons.
Argue, then collect any supporting citations.
Cite sources, then ignore them in reasoning.

questions.explanation: A sourced argument poses the question, gathers and weighs evidence, then argues; concluding or citing first reverses or empties the process.

questions.learningObjective: Read a text to extract its argument
questions.stem: When reading the memo for its argument, what should the translator extract first?

answer.exemplar: The translator should extract the conclusion and the reasons offered for it, then check whether the reasons support the conclusion and what assumptions bridge them.

questions.explanation: Reading for an argument starts with conclusion and reasons, then tests support and the bridging assumptions.

questions.topic: Turning a summary into a position
questions.learningObjective: Turn a neutral summary into a position
questions.stem: How can a neutral summary in the memo become a position?

options.text: By shortening it to one sentence.
By deleting all evidence and keeping opinions.
By adding an evaluative claim with supporting reasons.
By changing every noun to a stronger synonym.

questions.explanation: A position adds an evaluative claim backed by reasons; shortening or restyling does not create one.

questions.topic: Questions that rule out an answer
questions.learningObjective: Detect a question that excludes a possible answer

stimulus.body: The translator's note asks when the minister stopped lying, presupposing that the minister lied.

questions.stem: What is the flaw in the note's question?

options.text: It asks for a date that is easy to verify.
It uses a formal register.
It is too long to answer quickly.
It presupposes a contested claim and rules out innocence.

questions.explanation: The question presupposes lying and excludes the possibility of innocence; length and register are not the issue.

questions.topic: Removing the assumption from a question
questions.learningObjective: Rephrase a question to remove its assumption
questions.stem: How should the memo rephrase 'why did the reform fail?' to remove the assumption?

options.text: Why did the reform fail so completely?
Why did everyone dislike the reform?
Did the reform succeed or fail, and by what evidence?
Was the reform ever proposed?

questions.explanation: Removing the assumption means asking whether it succeeded or failed and on what evidence; strengthening or changing subject does not.

questions.topic: Crediting a change for what followed it
questions.learningObjective: Avoid crediting a change for later events
questions.stem: The memo credits a 2010 policy for growth in 2015; what must be checked?

options.text: Whether growth is measured in percent.
Whether the policy was popular in 2010.
Whether the policy's name sounds impressive.
Whether growth would have happened anyway.

questions.explanation: Crediting the policy requires checking whether the growth would have occurred without it; popularity and naming are irrelevant.

questions.learningObjective: Narrow a broad topic by adding constraints
questions.stem: Which constraint best narrows a broad topic about education without distorting it?

options.text: Limit to sources published on Tuesdays.
Limit to the author's personal opinion only.
Limit to one country, one decade, and one outcome measure.
Limit to topics the author already agrees with.

questions.explanation: Constraints on country, period, and outcome bound the inquiry without distorting it; opinion or arbitrary filters do.

questions.learningObjective: Judge answerability of a memo question
questions.stem: Why might a question about 19th-century wages be unanswerable from a parish register?

answer.exemplar: Parish registers record baptisms and burials, not wages, so a wage question lacks the needed variable in that source and must seek payrolls or account books.

questions.explanation: A source answers only questions about its recorded variables; wages need payroll records, not parish registers.

questions.learningObjective: Identify and fix a presupposing question
questions.stem: Which revision removes the presupposition from 'why is the plan wasteful?'?

options.text: Why is the plan so wasteful and harmful?
Why did anyone propose such waste?
How wasteful is the obviously bad plan?
Is the plan wasteful, and by what measure?

questions.explanation: Removing the presupposition asks whether the plan is wasteful and by what measure; other options keep or add it.

questions.learningObjective: Decide when a term needs definition

stimulus.body: The translator's note debates whether a policy is efficient without defining efficient.

questions.stem: What should the memo do before debating efficiency?

options.text: Vote on the most popular meaning of efficient.
Assume everyone means the same thing.
Define efficient with criteria and measurement.
Drop the term and use vague praise instead.

questions.explanation: Defining efficient with criteria and measurement prevents talking past each other; voting or assuming shared meaning does not.

questions.learningObjective: Handle a term lacking an equivalent
questions.stem: A term from physics has no equivalent in history; how should the translator proceed?

options.text: Force the physics term into history unchanged.
Replace it with an unrelated historical term.
Delete the concept from the history account.
Coin a gloss that explains the concept in historical terms.

questions.explanation: When no equivalent exists, a gloss in the target field's terms preserves meaning; forcing or deleting loses or distorts content.

questions.topic: Assumptions carried by a borrowed method
questions.learningObjective: Check assumptions of a borrowed method
questions.stem: The memo borrows a statistical test; what assumption must be verified first?

options.text: That the test's required distribution fits the data.
That the test was invented recently.
That the test's author is famous.
That the test uses Greek letters.

questions.explanation: A borrowed test requires checking its distributional assumptions; recency, fame, and notation are irrelevant.

questions.learningObjective: Mark where an analogy breaks down
questions.stem: The memo likens a market to an ecosystem; where does it break down?

options.text: At competition, since both involve rivalry.
At growth, since both grow over time.
At intention, since markets involve deliberate choice.
At diversity, since both have varied parts.

questions.explanation: Growth, competition, and diversity are shared; intention and deliberate choice mark where the ecosystem analogy breaks down.

questions.topic: The warrant joining claim to reason
questions.learningObjective: Supply a missing warrant
questions.stem: The memo gives reason 'traffic rose' and claim 'build a new road'; what warrant is missing?

answer.exemplar: The missing warrant is that rising traffic exceeds the existing road's capacity and that a new road would relieve it better than alternatives such as transit or pricing.

questions.explanation: The argument needs a warrant linking traffic growth to capacity limits and to the road as the best remedy; without it the leap is unsupported.

questions.topic: Unstated premises a reader must supply
questions.learningObjective: Identify a hidden premise

stimulus.body: The translator's note says the shop closed, so the owner retired, assuming no other reason for closing.

questions.stem: What hidden premise does the note rely on?

options.text: Shop closures always mean retirement.
Shops never reopen after closing.
All owners retire at the same age.
The owner had no other reason to close the shop.

questions.explanation: The inference needs the owner to lack other reasons to close; universal claims about retirement or reopening are too strong.

questions.learningObjective: Spot a non-following conclusion
questions.stem: Given that a drug passed a safety test, which conclusion does not follow?

options.text: The drug is unlikely to cause the tested harms.
The tested dose was tolerated.
The drug cures the target disease.
No severe tested reaction appeared.

questions.explanation: A safety test shows tolerated doses and absence of tested harms, not efficacy; curing the disease does not follow.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an additive objection
questions.stem: A critic adds a budget constraint not in the memo; how should the author respond?

options.text: Dismiss it as irrelevant without checking.
Attack the critic's motives.
Pretend the constraint was already addressed.
Weigh the new constraint against the plan's benefits.

questions.explanation: An additive objection deserves weighing against benefits; dismissal, pretense, or attack evade it.

questions.learningObjective: Adjudicate competing readings
questions.stem: When two readings conflict, what should settle it?

options.text: The reading better supported by context and usage.
The reading that matches the translator's preference.
The reading that is more dramatic.
The reading that cites more sources.

questions.explanation: Context and usage support one reading over another; preference, drama, and citation count do not.

questions.topic: Weight carried by primary and secondary sources
questions.learningObjective: Decide source weight for a factual claim
questions.stem: For a claim about what an author intended, which source should weigh more?

answer.exemplar: The author's own contemporary letters and drafts weigh more for intent than a later critic's summary, though the critic helps with broader reception.

questions.explanation: Contemporary authorial documents carry more weight for intent than later summaries, which serve reception instead.

questions.learningObjective: Check whether a summary preserves structure

stimulus.body: The translator's note summarizes the memo by listing only its final recommendation and omitting the reasons.

questions.stem: What is wrong with the note's summary?

options.text: It is too short to be useful.
It uses the wrong font.
It omits the reasons, breaking the argument structure.
It mentions the recommendation at all.

questions.explanation: Omitting reasons breaks the argument structure; length and formatting are not the issue.

questions.topic: Holding a position at its strongest
questions.learningObjective: Avoid weakening an opposing view
questions.stem: Which practice best avoids straw-manning an opposing view?

options.text: Ignore its supporting reasons entirely.
Quote only its weakest sentence.
Replace its terms with loaded ones.
Restate the view in its strongest form before critiquing.

questions.explanation: Restating the view at its strongest before critiquing prevents straw-manning; quoting weakness or distorting terms does not.

questions.learningObjective: Reconstruct a rejected view fairly
questions.stem: When reconstructing the rejected view, what must be included?

options.text: Personal details about its advocates.
Only its most absurd implication.
Its best arguments and the conclusion they aim at.
Unrelated facts to make it look weaker.

questions.explanation: Fair reconstruction includes the best arguments and their intended conclusion; caricature or personal details misrepresent it.

questions.topic: Sympathetic reading of a weak argument
questions.learningObjective: Read weak arguments charitably
questions.stem: What does charitable reading of a weak argument require?

options.text: Accepting its conclusion despite the flaws.
Dismissing the author as incompetent.
Rewriting it to agree with your view.
Identifying the insight or aim behind the flawed reasoning.

questions.explanation: Charitable reading identifies the insight or aim behind flawed reasoning without accepting the conclusion or attacking the author.

questions.topic: Citations that let a reader find the claim
questions.learningObjective: Improve an unlocatable citation
questions.stem: How should the memo fix a citation that only names an author?

answer.exemplar: Add the title, edition or volume, and page or paragraph range so a reader can locate the exact claim, plus a stable link if available.

questions.explanation: A locatable citation adds title, edition, and page or paragraph range; author alone leaves the claim unfindable.

questions.topic: Narrowing a topic in two steps
questions.learningObjective: Apply two-step narrowing

stimulus.body: The translator's note first limits the study to urban schools, then to reading scores.

questions.stem: What two-step narrowing does the note use?

options.text: It broadens the topic twice.
It deletes the topic and restarts.
It first bounds the population, then specifies the outcome.
It adds unrelated variables.

questions.explanation: The note first bounds population to urban schools, then specifies outcome to reading scores; broadening or restarting would not narrow.

questions.learningObjective: Order framing steps correctly
questions.stem: Which order correctly frames a research question?

options.text: Answer, then narrow, then define terms.
Conclude, then find reasons.
Cite sources, then invent the question.
Narrow topic, define terms, check answerability, refine.

questions.explanation: Correct framing narrows, defines, checks answerability, and refines; answering or concluding first reverses inquiry.
